abstract: Alpha-satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) arrays at human centromeres vary several-fold in length across individuals and have been linked to kinetochore function and chromosome missegregation. However, their repetitive megabase-scale architecture has largely restricted length measurement to a few hundred long-read derived genome assemblies, leaving short-read cohorts uncharacterized. Here we introduce cenlen, an alignment-free method that estimates active centromeric array lengths across all 24 human chromosomes directly from short-read or long-read CRAM files. To estimate array lengths, we first identify $k$-mers that are common within a query chromosome's centromere array but rare across other chromosomes. For acrocentric and other repeat-sharing families lacking private k-mers, cenlen instead models shared k-mer mixtures against assembled pangenome reference profiles using non-negative linear deconvolution. Across 61 genomes that were not used for training, cenlen estimates agreed closely with assembled array lengths (median relative error 2.4%), outperforming existing short-read estimators. We further optimized sequence retrieval and targeted k-mer counting, reducing CPU time 313-fold relative to existing methods. We applied cenlen to 2,557 individuals across genetic ancestries from the 1000 Genomes Project. Most variation in array length occurred within populations, but arrays on chr21, chr7 and chr16 differed between superpopulations more than the average common SNV. Finally, we found that array lengths were associated with molecular phenotypes, including splicing of MED14 in chromosome X. Overall, cenlen makes it possible to test associations between centromere array length variation and human traits in large sequencing cohorts.
